findings.claim: "Marx also used the concept of socio-economic classifications, recognising that in practice class positions are more complex than a simple two-class model"
findings.truth: Marx did not use socio-economic classifications. They are twentieth-century instruments (Registrar General's scale, NS-SEC). Marx did recognise groups between the two main classes, such as the petty bourgeoisie. The spec bullet 'socio-economic classifications and two class system' sits under Marxist theory, so the link is kept but the attribution is corrected.
findings.evidence: spec 5.1 required content; standard sociology of Marx's class model

findings.claim: "An examiner-flagged error is to describe any high-income person as 'high class' in Weber's terms"
findings.truth: No examiner source says this. Fabricated examiner claims are barred; the point stands as a common student error.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: "The mark scheme rewards candidates who systematically compare the consensus view ... with conflict views"
findings.truth: An invented claim about an unseen mark scheme. Reworded as advice about strong answers.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims and copyright distancing

findings.claim: "The 2024 examiner report noted that stronger candidates understood that functionalists accept power differences exist but see them as 'inevitable and necessary' for the smooth running of society."
findings.truth: There is no such examiner report finding, and the quoted words are invented. The sociological point itself is sound and is kept without the false source.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims and invented mark-scheme quotations

findings.claim: "Max Weber (1947) distinguished three distinct types of authority"
findings.truth: Weber died in 1920. 1947 is the date of the English translation of Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft (1922). Beside 'Davis and Moore (1945)' in the same unit, the date reads as a publication by a living author and implies Weber wrote after them.
findings.evidence: Weber 1864-1920; Economy and Society published posthumously 1922, Parsons translation 1947

findings.claim: "A police officer who physically restrains someone exercises power; a judge who imposes a sentence exercises authority"
findings.truth: Police restraint is legitimate force exercised under law, so it is authority, not bare power. Weber's own definition gives the state a monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force, and the same lesson later lists the police as a formal agency of social control with legally defined powers. The example is swapped for one of illegitimate power.
findings.evidence: Weber's definition of the state; internal contradiction with the lesson's own agencies-of-social-control section

findings.claim: "The mark scheme expects: the correct name (1 mark), the source of legitimacy explained (1 mark), and a developed example (1 mark)."
findings.truth: An invented mark allocation for an unseen mark scheme. The advice is kept as a description of a full answer.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims and copyright distancing

findings.claim: "Devine's study is important for Eduqas/WJEC students because it challenges ..."
findings.truth: Student-facing prose must never name the board. This is the only occurrence in the unit.
findings.evidence: house rule (Eduqas/WJEC never named in prose)

findings.claim: "The MacPherson Report (1999)"
findings.truth: The report is the Macpherson Report, by Sir William Macpherson, February 1999. The year is right; only the capitalisation of the name is wrong.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia: Macpherson Report (Stephen Lawrence Inquiry, February 1999)

findings.claim: "The mark scheme rewards sociological vocabulary and explanation of mechanisms"
findings.truth: An invented claim about an unseen mark scheme.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: "women continue to carry a disproportionate share of domestic labour and childcare (Oakley's double shift)"
findings.truth: Oakley (1974) documented the dual burden of housework and paid work, but the term 'double shift' / 'second shift' is Hochschild's (1989). The attribution is loose rather than wrong, and Oakley is a spec-named thinker, so it is recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: Oakley, The Sociology of Housework 1974; Hochschild, The Second Shift 1989

findings.claim: "The specification explicitly names Islamophobia and antisemitism as documented forms of religious inequality."
findings.truth: The spec names neither term. Section 5.3 carries a single bullet, 'religion and belief'. Both are legitimate teaching examples, but they are not spec-named, so the framing is corrected.
findings.evidence: spec 5.3 required content (grep for 'islamophob' and 'antisemit' returns nothing)

findings.claim: "Young people below the age of 18 cannot vote and have limited political power."
findings.truth: 16- and 17-year-olds vote in Senedd and local elections in Wales (Senedd and Elections (Wales) Act 2019) and in Scottish Parliament and local elections in Scotland. The age of 18 applies to UK general elections. This matters for a Welsh board's students.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Voting age: UK general elections 18; Wales and Scotland devolved and local elections 16

findings.claim: "Goldthorpe and Lockwood studied male manual workers at the Vauxhall car plant in Luton, arguing that affluent workers were becoming embourgeoisified"
findings.truth: Reversed. The Affluent Worker study tested the embourgeoisement thesis and rejected it. Workers had not become middle class; Goldthorpe and Lockwood described a new working-class outlook, privatised instrumentalism. The lesson's own Devine section, and Lesson 3, both depend on that rejection, so the paragraph contradicts the rest of the unit.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia (John Goldthorpe): the research 'called into question the idea of the embourgeoisement of the British working class'; Goldthorpe 1967, The Affluent Worker and the Theory of Embourgeoisement

findings.claim: "The mark scheme rewards depth, not breadth."
findings.truth: An invented claim about an unseen mark scheme.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Practice question 1 and one flashcard date Devine's Luton fieldwork to "the early 1990s"; the lesson body dates it to the late 1980s.
findings.truth: Devine's interviews ran in 1986-87 and Affluent Workers Revisited was published in 1992. The body text is right and the answer (Devine) is unaffected, so this is recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: Devine, Affluent Workers Revisited, 1992

findings.claim: Practice question 3: "Identify and describe Townsend's concept of the 'cycle of deprivation'."
findings.truth: The cycle of deprivation is not Townsend's concept; it was coined by Sir Keith Joseph in 1972 and the spec lists it unattributed. Townsend's concept is relative deprivation, measured by his deprivation index. The lesson body correctly leaves the cycle unattributed, so only the question stem misattributes it.
findings.evidence: spec 5.5 lists 'cycle of deprivation' as a bare bullet and attributes only relative deprivation to Townsend

findings.claim: "The mark scheme expects a sociological definition"
findings.truth: An invented claim about an unseen mark scheme.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: "Students should be careful not to conflate the two in a 2-mark Define answer - each definition earns a separate mark."
findings.truth: An invented mark allocation, and confused: a 2-mark Define question asks for one term, so two definitions cannot each earn a mark. Recorded rather than edited because no clean surgical replacement keeps the sentence's teaching point.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: "this scores in the lower band. The mark scheme rewards depth"
findings.truth: An invented claim about an unseen mark scheme.
findings.evidence: house rule on fabricated examiner claims

findings.claim: Unit-wide: every lesson teaches a fixed question ladder of 1, 2, 3, 4, 9 and 12 marks (Multiple Choice, Define, Identify and Describe, Describe, Discuss, Evaluate).
findings.truth: The spec does not print a question ladder. Nothing here contradicts the published facts (written exam 1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks, 50% of the qualification, AO1 40 / AO2 40 / AO3 20, at least 15% of marks on research methods), and no tariff is impossible, so the ladder is recorded as unverifiable rather than edited.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 and 3.1

summary: Two reversed or misplaced attributions drive the unit: Goldthorpe and Lockwood are credited with the embourgeoisement thesis they actually rejected (L5), and a practice question hands Townsend the cycle of deprivation (L6). The rest is a run of fabricated examiner and mark-scheme claims across six lessons, one board name in prose (L3), and two false spec claims. All named thinkers, Walby's six structures, Weber's three authority types, the Equality Act 2010 and Townsend's 22% / 6% figures check out.
